answer:
**Verdict:** No, not in the sense of treating it as a company. Keep building the side project, and make it a company only if it takes off by itself. His rule for a 20-year-old is that a startup and being a student don't mix, so don't set out to start one. His exception covers your situation: if a side project takes off, "maybe it's reasonable to run with it."

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: high). He gave this rule and exception in 2014 and held the rule in 2026. He never addressed your exact case, a student excited about a side project, so applying it to you is my inference.

**How we get there**
1. **The rule.** "Do not start a startup in college." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 18:56, [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1136s)). His reason: "though starting a startup could be a good thing to do at some point, 20 is not the optimal time to do it." He adds that "You're not sacrificing anything if you forego starting a startup at 20, cuz you'll be more likely to succeed if you wait." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 21:12).
2. **The exception.** If a project takes off on its own, "Then you face the choice of either running with it or not, and maybe it's reasonable to run with it." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 21:12, [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1272s)). He says startups should come from side projects. "None of these companies were even supposed to be companies at first, they were all just side projects." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 25:08). You'll know it's becoming a startup "when it takes over an alarming percentage of your life" ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 43:15).
3. **The 2026 update.** His August 2026 essay keeps the rule: "Running a startup is incompatible with being a full time student." ([[web-c75e015ff81a]], [essay](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html)). But he now puts the weight on side projects. He wants universities to give students free time because "a significant number of those side projects would be incipient startups". He also notes that Microsoft and Meta both started in Harvard's reading period, and asks "Are the students just supposed to abandon them? Because it's either that or drop out."
4. **Applied to you.** An exciting side project at 20 is the case he describes. Work on it, learn from it, and see whether it pulls you in. Don't incorporate, raise money, or drop out until it does.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Waiting is cheap.** Your early twenties are for open-ended exploration that success would end. He lists "plunge deeply into projects on a whim that seem like they have no payoff" ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 19:32). Of Facebook, he says "success has taken a lot of the serendipity out of his life" ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 20:40).
- **Startups consume you.** "Startups are all consuming. If you start a start up, it will take over your life to a degree that you cannot imagine." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 14:28). That is why it doesn't fit with a degree.
- **Learn powerful things now.** For college he says "just learn" ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 30:49). In 2026 he still says to study CS, because "The hard part of startups is product" ([[web-c75e015ff81a]]).
- **Risk early.** "The solution is to take multiple shots. Which is another reason to start taking risks early." ([[web-76d87c7c2e80]], [essay](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)). The young "can afford to risk trying it to find out" (same essay). This pulls toward trying. It is why the project is worth doing, but it doesn't change the "not as a student" part.

**What he's done:** He doesn't give his own story here. He started YC "because it seemed interesting" ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 27:23), which matches his curiosity-first line.

**What would change his answer:**
- **Traction.** If real users want it, growth is fast, and it's taking over your life, he'd say run with it. He doesn't say whether you'd then drop out, only that "it's either that or drop out."
- **Loose end in his views.** In the same 2014 Q&A he says "the best way to learn how to start a startup is to try and start it", and in 2026 "The only way to learn how to start a startup is to do it." That sits uneasily with "wait." He never reconciles the two. If you want to find out whether you can do it, he says "the only way to find out is to try, just not now" ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 23:58), so a side project is the way to test it.

**Caveat:** The 2014 "don't" was said to Stanford students, and the 2026 essay is addressed to universities rather than to students. He also speaks as YC's founder with a stake in the model: he calls YC where students go next ("We're like grad school") and says the only proper startup class is YC ([[web-c75e015ff81a]]; see [[profile]]).

**My own view, separate from his:** A strong rule of "wait" is easy to defend when a YC batch will still be there in two years. If your project is attracting users now, I'd weigh that more heavily than the age rule.

**Verdict:** No, he doesn't think you have to move for good, but he does think you should go. His answer to this question, given in Stockholm, was: "Yes, you should. You can go there for a bit and then come back, but you should at least go." Treat it as a strong "should", not a "must".

**Based on:** said it. He gave this talk to a Stockholm audience (April 2026), and the vault has no earlier or conflicting PG statement to weigh against it.

**Why he'd say it**
- He treats this as an old question that applies to every field, not a Silicon Valley quirk: "Should I go there? And the answer is the same now as it always is. Yes, you should. You can go there for a bit and then come back, but you should at least go." ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 0:36, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=36s)
- **Peers and chance meetings:** "You get the best peers. And in fact, the talent pool expands in two dimensions. The people are better, and there's also a lot more of them." ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 1:09, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=69s)
- **The effect on you:** "the biggest advantage of moving to one of these centers is not what it does for you, but what it does to you." ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 8:19, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=499s) He means that seeing big fish up close makes the goal feel "just a hard one" rather than impossible.
- **Fundraising:** "Investors outside Silicon Valley implicitly assume that any local startup is second rate." ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 6:39, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=399s) "if you leave for Silicon Valley, you make this rule operate in reverse. You automatically rise in investors' opinion." Even a short stint raises your standing back home.
- **The best way to do it is YC:** "Surely the optimal way to go to Silicon Valley for a bit and then come back is to do YC." ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 17:16, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1036s)

**Where he stops short of "must":** He says himself that startups going home after YC are "only about half as likely to become unicorns" ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 18:57, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1137s). He then gives three reasons not to be discouraged:
1. Selection bias: more confident and determined founders are the ones who move abroad.
2. The figure measures valuation, not performance.
3. "even if you only do half as well, that's still pretty good."

He adds "Money isn't everything" and mentions caring more about your kids than your company ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 19:30, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1170s). So he treats staying home as a real cost but a survivable one.

He also wants you to come back, because it helps Stockholm: "as long as you do actually come back, that's one of the best things you can do to help Sweden to help Stockholm thrive as a startup hub." ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 16:10, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=970s)

**What they've done:** YC has long made founders come to the Valley. Its Boston batches were flown out to Silicon Valley for a second demo day because Boston investors wouldn't fund them ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 7:43).

**Discount for who's talking:** The vault's profile page flags this talk as PG "talking my own book". He says as much himself ("I know it will sound like I'm talking my own book at this point"), and YC profits from founders making the trip. The unicorn figure is YC's own data, given without method ([[profile]]).

**What would change his answer:** He gives no explicit condition under which he'd say "stay". His own logic suggests two, but those are my reading, not his words:
- If your market or customers are local and you can't use the Valley's peers or investors.
- If the cost to your family is too high, since he says money isn't everything.

**Altman's view:** Sam Altman (July 2026) agrees, less firmly. He says moving to the Bay Area was the best way to find people to start a startup with, but that he has "less of an intuition for it now" ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]], [[startups/location/should-you-move-to-silicon-valley]]).

The practical read is a trip, not a relocation: a stint in the Valley, ideally through YC, then back to Stockholm if you want.

**Verdict:** Seibel would tell you to stop optimizing the deck and the meeting circuit, and go make the company grow fast enough that investors chase you. He'd say months of pitching without a close means you're in a low-leverage fundraise. The deck and the follow-ups can't fix that.

His first question wouldn't be about your deck. He says that when founders asked "how do I raise a good round" or "what should be in my pitch deck," he'd stop them and ask: "how much leverage do you have?" Investors respond to growth, not to the deck.

**Based on:** said it. The October 2026 Dalton + Michael episode (the vault's most recent source) describes your situation directly. Confidence is high. The one thing I don't know is your growth, and his answer turns on that (see the last section).

**Why he'd say it**
- **Time is the cost.** Seibel spent about eight months trying to raise for Justin.tv. When it was clear the money wasn't coming and two months of runway were left, they had to make the company profitable. He says they got more done in those two months than in the eight. "we got to figure out how to make this thing profitable or we're going to die." ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 6:44, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=404s))
- **Long fundraises are a drag.** "if you just think about how much time is wasted, it's like a it's like a drag on the industry." ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 6:44) He's describing a "low leverage fundraiser" where "there's no way it's going to work, but you just go through months and months and months of pitching."
- **Investors chase.** He asked investors who now want to back him what share of their deals they chase versus get through the front door. The answers were 80/20 to 90/10 in favor of chasing. His conclusion: "if you can invest that time in making your company something that investors will chase after versus decksmithing, you're you're playing into the odds versus playing out of the odds." ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 10:03, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=603s))
- **Traction made the deck irrelevant.** When Socialcam was "the number two app in the app store," one of their decks "kind of just was like here's some questions you can ask us." ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 9:30)
- **A bad fundraiser with traction beats a great one without.** Caldwell, his co-host, puts it as "way better to be like a very bad fundraiser" with something that works ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 5:35). Both credit the idea to Paul Graham, who said it in 2014: "the best way to convince investors, is to start a startup that's actually doing well, meaning ... growing fast, and then simply tell investors so." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 9:51, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=591s))
- **It's an old view.** In 2019 Seibel said "spending all that time on a pitch deck is not as valuable as spending your time building anything that you can give to a customer." ([[yt-1hHMwLxN6EM]] @ 11:11, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=671s)) That was about MVPs, but it's the same idea. I found no source where he changed his mind.

**On the follow-up meetings:** one of the hosts (the transcript doesn't say which) explains why investors keep taking meetings. Most VCs invest on traction, so stringing a founder along is like buying an option: if you take off, they're well positioned. The host says those meetings then harm "their ability to create that inflection point" ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 8:57). A string of "keep us posted" meetings isn't a sign of interest.

**What he'd have you do** (follows from what they said, medium confidence on the specifics)
1. Ask yourself the leverage question: "if any deal dies how much do you care" ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 13:23, Caldwell). That line is about sales, but Seibel says fundraising works the same way. If one investor passing would hurt, you're not in a strong position.
2. Spend the hours on building, launching, talking to users and growing. They estimate how much value founders would have created with the hours they spent on a seed round ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 6:10).
3. Don't wait on one investor. Seibel says founders with a hot sales deal stop doing outreach, and the same habit applies to a "promising" investor ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 12:51).
4. Go back out once you have numbers going up, and keep the raise short. They say you can be "really bad at fundraising" and do it "in a very short time frame" if growth is strong enough.

**What would change his answer**
- If you're **already growing fast** and investors are circling, a process makes sense. The leverage is real and the work is closing it.
- If you're **not growing or haven't launched**, he'd be harsher. Someone in the episode says working on the deck is "the biggest waste of your time" in that case (speaker not clear, [[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 2:48).
- Caldwell is a partner at Standard Capital, a Series A fund that sponsors the show, and he holds up its capped-time process as the model. So the "investors should respect founders' time" part comes from an interested party. The "growth beats the deck" part is independent: PG said it in 2014.

**One disagreement, mine and not in the vault:** "just grow first" assumes you can show traction before you have money. For hardware or deep-tech founders, that may not be possible.

**Verdict:** Seibel would tell you to stop trading letters now. Move to a one-week, roughly $2,000 clean separation in which your cofounder gives back most of his vested stock, down to under 5% of the company. At 9 months in, he'd likely aim for 1–2%. Add reasonable severance and clean paperwork. His reasoning is that before product-market fit the stock is nearly worthless, so you're fighting over ego and the lawyers are the only ones who get paid.

**Based on:** said it. He addressed this exact situation: pre-PMF, vested stock, lawyers. It comes from a single episode, so no other source corroborates it. That is the Dalton + Michael episode "Do You Need a Co-Founder for Your Startup?" ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]], 2026-07-13, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U). Most of the quote attributions are medium confidence, because the speaker is assigned by continuity.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Time:** "when you really know the probability of success is zero, most important thing is to stop wasting time." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 9:26, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=566s). He says many founders live in a phase where they haven't decided to break up yet, though everyone knows it's over.
- **Lawyers:** "in a situation where you're having a co-founder breakup and the stock is worth nothing, paying lawyers a bunch of money makes no sense." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 11:36, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=696s). He adds that "a lawyer can suck up infinite amount of your ... anger and monetize it." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 12:07). He has seen founders end up in debt over a company that's worth nothing.
- **Why he wants the stock back:** "the vast majority of the value this company could create hasn't been created yet." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 14:47, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=887s). Whoever stays needs the equity to motivate themselves and future hires. The leaver gets a free hedge: "Like, you get to hedge. The founder staying doesn't." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 15:21).
- **The numbers:** "even if you vested, like get down to under 5% of the company, if it's within the first year, under 2%." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 18:39, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1119s). Later he says: "After a number of years, 5% typical. Under a year, 1%, 2%, sometimes less than 1%." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 21:22; high confidence).
- **The package:** "Do reasonable severance, sign clean paperwork and and peace out" and "you could do that whole thing in a week and spend like $2,000." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 18:39).
- **How to behave:** the staying founder should be "the responsible party". He says "it is so cheap to be nice" and that "everyone in your company is looking at you right now." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 17:33, @ 18:06). Lawyers who tell you to "protect yourself" can trigger the fight you're trying to avoid.
- **Fault:** Caldwell says to go no-fault, "Don't try to ruin the other person. Don't try to ruin the reputation." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 13:42). Seibel is blunter: "If you made a list of all the things we screwed up in our company, it would be way longer than the things you're pissed at your co-founder about." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 21:54; high confidence).

**What to do with the lawyers you already have** (inferred from his lawyer warnings, not stated for this case)
1. Redirect both lawyers from correspondence to one set of exit documents. Seibel doesn't say never to use lawyers. He says not to pay them to fight.
2. Don't make any mediator or advisor the judge: "If you're using someone to mediate this, don't make them the judge." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 19:46). The facts of who did what don't matter.
3. Seibel says he often talks to the leaving founder first and makes the case for leaving equity with the people who stay. You could do the same, or have someone you both trust do it. Offer generous severance if the company can afford it.
4. If the company is dead rather than just the partnership, the vault only says to stop wasting time. Treat the split the same way: fast, cheap and clean.

**What they've done:** Seibel says YC has these breakup standards written down, so a partner gives both cofounders the same advice. He also says his own first company had four cofounders, "two and a half" of them engaged at any given time.

**What would change his answer**
- **Misconduct:** "if your co-founder is breaking the law, doing something unethical, killing people, none of this applies." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 21:54). Caldwell similarly excludes felonies. Then he'd say to call the lawyers.
- **Product-market fit:** the advice is explicitly for pre-PMF companies. If the stock had real value, the logic of fighting over nothing would no longer hold.
- **Which side you're on:** I assumed you're the one staying. If you're the one leaving, he says to remember that the team needs to be motivated to make your remaining stock worth something.

**Where the vault is silent** (not in the vault): Seibel never says what to do if the cofounder flatly refuses to give stock back. These percentages are YC norms, not legal rights. Unless your documents give the company a repurchase right, vested shares generally belong to him. That is why this needs a negotiated deal rather than an ultimatum, and it's a question for your lawyer.

**One caveat on the source:** the episode is sponsored by Standard Capital, Caldwell's fund, and this is an investor's view of what matters, which is the company's equity pool. A cofounder who has put in nine months may reasonably see the fairness question differently, but that's my read, not Seibel's.

**Correction first:** Garry Tan didn't say this. Sam Altman did, in conversation with Tan at the close of Startup School 2026, and he says outright that Tan couldn't say it: "I can say this, Gary probably can't." Tan was the host. The vault has no statement from Tan making the "premium" claim.

**Verdict:** Altman says the premium grew because of network effects. YC's network of founders and alumni compounds as it gets bigger, so it pulls further ahead of anything that competes with it.

**Based on:** said it, though thinly. He gives one reason, network effects, and doesn't develop it with specifics.

**What he said** ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1016s), [[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]] @ 16:56; by: altman; conf: high):
> "I also think that I I can say this, Gary probably can't. I I I think the premium on doing YC is bigger now than it's like ever been before. Uh, the distance between like YC and second place is has expanded. And this is a reminder of the power of network effects."

He goes straight on to say you should find networks that help you meet your eventual co-founders, because "it takes a long time to compound" (@ 17:28).

**How he got there**
- The question was how to find your people. He said moving to the Bay Area used to work like magic: "You got a lot of like lucky chances and collisions" (@ 16:56). In his telling, that kind of density is what YC now supplies.
- He treats the widening gap to second place as proof that network effects compound. The more people in the network, the more valuable it is to join, and a rival can't catch up simply by copying the program.
- He draws the practical lesson for founders: join networks early, because they compound slowly.

**What Tan added:** Tan didn't comment on the premium. About six minutes later he described "this kind of like loose network and the spirit of helping each other and this like very long-term outlook" as "an awesome thing" ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]] @ 23:35; by: tan; conf: high). Just before that, he said "when you join YC it's like even more rarified" (@ 23:03). That supports the network-effects reading but isn't a separate argument.

**A related point from PG (not about the premium):** PG's 2026 essay says "YC itself is an instance of network effects in something you wouldn't expect to have them. We didn't intend it to be, but we realized very quickly that that was what we'd stumbled upon." ([paulgraham.com/powerful](https://paulgraham.com/powerful.html), [[web-19ac0b6d18d2]]; by: pg; conf: high). That fits Altman's explanation, but PG wasn't explaining the recent growth in the gap.

**Caveats the vault flags**
- Altman is a former YC president speaking at YC's own event, so he has a stake in the claim. He says as much himself.
- Nobody gives a figure or any evidence for the gap. It's an assertion.
- Altman hedges on the Bay Area advice: "I feel like I have less of an intuition for it now."

**What would change the answer:** If the claim is meant to say something beyond network effects, such as AI-era batch quality or better alumni outcomes, the vault doesn't back that as Altman's reasoning. Tan makes those arguments elsewhere, but not as an explanation of the gap.

**Verdict:** The premise is backwards. The vault has no statement from Livingston that early YC deliberately backed the most aggressive, ruthless founders. She says nearly the opposite. She screened out conceited founders, and she used "aggressive" and "ruthless" for the investors YC was different from, not for the founders she funded.

**Based on:** said it. She addressed this directly, and the vault has no source that supports the claim.

**What she said**
- She called the investors of the time aggressive and ruthless, and presented herself as the contrast. In her 2018 talk she says: "I was soft and sensitive at a time when investors tended to be hardened and aggressive and I'll throw in ruthless" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 17:44; by: livingston; conf: high). [Video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1064s). She follows it with how she looked after founders: she asked whether they were overwhelmed or eating properly, and she helped with co-founder disputes.
- She funded only earnest people. "From the beginning I was very careful about only funding earnest people" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 14:51; by: livingston; conf: high). [Video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=891s).
- She turned down conceited applicants and credits that with YC's culture: "if I could tell someone was a conceited we did not fund them", and "early on I was pretty rigid about this and I think that's the basis of the culture of our alumni community" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 15:27; by: livingston; conf: high). [Video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=927s). She concedes YC has since funded some conceited founders.
- In 2024 she repeated the earnest theme: "Earnest and not pretentious that's in YC's DNA" ([[yt-6u4JVz7iQTY]] @ 45:34; by: livingston; conf: high).

**Where the claim may come from**
- **Risk-taking:** she says having no LPs let YC "take more risks with who we chose to fund" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 19:26). The risk she describes is young and unconventional founders, not ruthless ones. She says YC had "more faith in young founders than most investors did" and judged them "not by what they were but what they could turn into".
- **Determination and boldness:** her traits are "determined" and "flexible minded". She wants "a certain amount of boldness to work on ideas that most people would consider stupid" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 25:45), plus "unconventional you know independent-minded" founders ([[yt-6u4JVz7iQTY]] @ 19:17). That is persistence under ridicule, not aggression toward other people.
- **PG's "formidable":** the toughness-wins idea sits closer to Paul Graham than to her. He says "that's why investors want people who are formidable" ([[yt-5bxp78i96S8]] @ 9:57; by: pg; conf: high), and that the hardest part of judging founders was predicting "how tough and ambitious they would become" ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 22:52; by: pg; conf: high). His formidable founder is someone who gets what they want in any situation. That is not the same as ruthless, and it is his view, not hers.

**What they've done:** In interviews she sat silently, read the founders' character and the relationship between the co-founders, and then told her partners whether to fund them. She also helped get a failing startup's founders hired at a big company, which brought her and PG into conflict with an investor ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 19:26).

**What would change this answer:** a source where she explicitly says tough or ruthless founders win. I searched the wiki and the raw transcripts for "ruthless" and "aggressive" and found nothing like that. If you remember it from a specific interview, tell me which one. It may not be in the vault, or the speaker may have been misattributed.
